answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: The exact wording appears as No. 560 (numbered 660 in this particular scan) in Thomas Fuller’s 1732 Gnomologia ↗, so the phrase is genuine and correctly linked to his book. But Fuller compiled proverbs rather than coining them ↗ — he recorded an already-circulating saying whose original author is anonymous.

author.name: Thomas Fuller
author.heading: About Thomas Fuller
author.bio: Thomas Fuller (1654–1734) was an English physician trained at Queens’ College, Cambridge, who is best remembered not for medicine but for two anthologies of proverbs and maxims: Introductio ad Prudentiam (1726–27) and the massive Gnomologia: Adagies and Proverbs (1732). He was a collector of sayings, gathering ancient, foreign and British adages into numbered lists — which is why phrases ‘from Fuller’ are often folk proverbs he preserved rather than lines he invented. He is frequently confused with the earlier churchman-historian Thomas Fuller (1608–1661).

misattribution.heading: Who it’s wrongly pinned on
misattribution.intro: Two attribution problems attach to this proverb: crediting Fuller as its author, and a separate false trail to the Persian poet Saadi.

items.why: Fuller’s Gnomologia is where the earliest match appears, so quoting ‘Thomas Fuller’ as the source of the book is fair. But Fuller was, per Quote Investigator ↗, ‘primarily a collector and not a crafter of sayings’ — he recorded a proverb already in circulation, so treating him as the mind who coined it overstates the record.

Some sources credit the 13th-century Persian poet Saadi. Quote Investigator ↗ shows this began with Moncure Conway’s 1874 Sacred Anthology, which printed ‘Have patience! All things are difficult before they become easy’ just before a Saadi passage — the adage ‘does not appear in the text by Saadi’ but later readers (including Forbes) misread the layout and attached it to him.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest verdict: a genuine old proverb, first documented in Thomas Fuller’s 1732 Gnomologia ↗ — Fuller preserved it, but its original author is anonymous, and it is not Saadi’s.

context.heading: Why it reads as wisdom
lead: The line survives because it compresses a universal experience of learning into six beats: the gap between a skill’s first, clumsy attempt and its eventual ease. That is exactly the kind of tidy, memorable maxim Fuller’s Gnomologia was built to preserve — a numbered warehouse of ‘wise sentences and witty sayings’ drawn from ancient, foreign and British sources.
detailsBody: Gnomologia (1732) collects several thousand short adages, each numbered. Because Fuller drew on older proverb stock, many entries have deep pre-1732 roots in English and continental proverb collections, and individual authorship is usually untraceable — which is precisely why Quote Investigator lands on ‘anonymous’ for this line rather than on Fuller himself.
context.pull: Fuller kept the proverb; he did not coin it.
